articles.deck: Michael Loconto — Pro Tour New York 1996
articles.era: 1996 Pro Tour New York-era Standard under current milling terminology
articles.title: Two cards gone before the next draw
articles.intro: Millstone changes the library, not the player's hand. Its two-mana tap activation mills two cards from the top of one targeted player's library into their graveyard; winning by decking still requires that player to attempt a draw from an empty library.
articles.lesson: Pay {2} and tap Millstone to make its target player mill two cards. The player doesn't discard cards from hand, Millstone doesn't itself draw any cards, and milling the last cards doesn't immediately make a player lose the game.
articles.origin: Kaja Foglio illustrated the original Millstone in Antiquities. The card gave patient control players an alternate way to win after stabilizing the battlefield, even when the library itself was otherwise untouched.
articles.technical: Millstone can activate on an opponent's end step because an artifact's tap ability is not restricted by sorcery timing. If a player has exactly two cards left, both can go to their graveyard; they lose only when they later try to draw from an empty library, barring replacement effects.
articles.history: The documentary Michael Loconto 1996 Pro Tour New York white-blue control list includes Millstone, Jayemdae Tome and Counterspell. The following opponent library state is deliberately reconstructed, not a tournament game report.
articles.story: On my opponent's end step, I tapped two [[Island]]s to pay for [[Millstone]], then tapped the artifact and targeted my opponent. They had two cards left in their library. Both cards went to the graveyard, and their hand did not change. I still had [[Counterspell]] for a possible answer, but the opponent did not lose just because their library was empty. On their next draw step, if nothing replaced or prevented the empty-library draw, they would lose while trying to draw. Millstone had created that problem without dealing a point of damage.
articles.review: {2} paid by two Islands. Millstone itself taps and mills exactly two from a 2-card opponent library. Empty library does not immediately cause a loss; player loses on attempted draw. Exact match fictional.

articles.era: 1994 U.S. Nationals Type I control inspired representative table
articles.matchup: Mind Twist/Rack Control against creature pressure
articles.title: Seven cards became three life
articles.intro: Ivory Tower rewards a full hand at the beginning of upkeep. It gains life equal to the number of cards currently in hand beyond four, if any, before the ordinary draw step begins.
articles.lesson: The Tower's triggered ability resolves during its controller's upkeep; the life gained is the controller's current hand size minus four (minimum zero life gained). It does not tap, draw a card, or count the card to be drawn later in the draw step.
articles.origin: Margaret Organ-Kean's original Ivory Tower appeared in Antiquities. Decks capable of keeping a large hand could turn this seemingly passive artifact into an ongoing buffer against aggressive clocks.
articles.technical: A player beginning upkeep with seven cards in hand gains three life from a single Tower, moving from nine life to twelve. The normal draw follows later; playing cards between upkeeps reduces later Tower gains.
articles.history: The preserved Bo Bell 1994 Mind Twist/Rack Control archive is documented as an unusual 65-card main deck and includes Ivory Tower, Ancestral Recall and The Rack. The invented seven-card hand is not attributed to an actual Nationals game.
articles.story: I reached my upkeep with seven cards in hand and [[Ivory Tower]] on the battlefield. My opponent had been attacking through my defenses, leaving me at nine life. The Tower trigger counted seven cards, subtracted four, and gave me three life, moving me to twelve. Only after that did I go to my draw step and draw normally. [[Ancestral Recall]] remained among the options in my hand, and [[The Rack]] was already pressuring the other side. The Tower had not tapped or drawn anything; it merely paid me for holding cards at the right moment.
articles.review: Seven hand cards at Tower trigger resolution, gain 7-4=3 life, 9->12, before normal draw. Does not tap or grant extra draw. Source deck contains Tower, Ancestral Recall, The Rack. 65-card original documented main.

articles.era: 1995 World Championship-era Standard illustration using modern timing
articles.matchup: Rack Control against white land-destruction control
articles.title: The lands were gone, but the life was mine
articles.intro: Zuran Orb turns lands into two life each without requiring mana or tapping the artifact. Sacrificing a land is an activation cost, so a destroyed or countered ability cannot bring that land back.
articles.lesson: Zuran Orb costs {0} to cast and has an activated ability with 'Sacrifice a land' as its entire cost. Each resolution gains two life. It can be activated in response to a spell such as Armageddon, but doing so permanently removes those lands before Armageddon resolves.
articles.origin: Sandra Everingham illustrated Zuran Orb for Ice Age in 1995, giving players a direct way to convert mana development into emergency life. The land sacrifice is an economic choice rather than free infinite lifegain.
articles.technical: When Armageddon is cast, a player can sacrifice a Plains and a Swamp to Zuran Orb while it remains on the stack. Each activation grants two life on resolution, gaining four in total. Armageddon later destroys the lands still on the battlefield; previously sacrificed lands are already gone.
articles.history: The Alexander Blumke 1995 Rack Control archive contains Zuran Orb, Swamps, Plains and The Rack. The opposing Armageddon is a constructed period-plausible choice and not a documented moment from the final.
articles.story: My opponent cast [[Armageddon]], and I had [[Zuran Orb]] on the battlefield with a [[Plains]] and [[Swamp]] still untapped. Before Armageddon resolved, I sacrificed both lands to Orb in separate activations. I gained two life from each ability, taking my total from six to ten. The sacrificed lands had already gone to the graveyard; Armageddon could not destroy them a second time. I kept [[The Rack]] in play, but I had also surrendered both mana sources. Orb did not tap, and none of that life arrived because I had paid mana to activate it.
articles.review: Armageddon on stack, Orb sacrifice of Plains/Swamp as two separate costs, 2+2 lifegain from 6->10 before Armageddon. Lands gone before sweep, Orb stays. Opponent invented, named deck contains Orb/Rack/lands.

articles.era: 1995 Worlds Standard using contemporary card pool and current resolution
articles.title: Two cards taken without choosing either
articles.intro: Hymn to Tourach spends two black mana to make one target player discard two cards at random, a distinction from deliberate hand disruption such as Duress. It can remove a critical card through chance, not perfect information.
articles.lesson: Hymn to Tourach is a {B}{B} sorcery targeting a player. That player discards two random cards from their current hand as the spell resolves, or as many as they have if fewer than two. The caster does not choose particular cards, and cards aren't milled from the library.
articles.origin: Fallen Empires debuted multiple original print artworks of Hymn to Tourach in 1994. The 38a variation is illustrated by Susan Van Camp; other distinct original copies have other artists and should not be silently mislabeled.
articles.technical: With two untapped Swamps, the caster can pay {B}{B}. If the target opponent holds exactly three cards on resolution, randomly select two distinct cards to discard into their graveyard, leaving one card in hand. The Rack may pressure the smaller hand afterward but does not change which cards Hymn chooses.
articles.history: The Alexander Blumke 1995 World Championship Rack Control archive contains Hymn to Tourach and The Rack. The specific hand contents in the vignette are fictitious and do not reflect a reported match or known random outcome.
articles.story: I tapped two [[Swamp]]s during my main phase and cast [[Hymn to Tourach]] at my opponent, who had three cards in hand. They shuffled the cards face down, and two were selected at random for discard. I had not chosen their strongest spells, and the remaining card was not automatically the worst. [[The Rack]] was already on my battlefield, ready to punish a small hand on a later trigger. Hymn left one card in their hand and none in exile. I watched the discarded cards go to the graveyard and knew that random was the entire point of the spell.
articles.review: Two Swamps produce BB, sorcery on caster main phase, three cards opponent hand, two random discard leaving one, no chosen-target-cards or library mill. Rack remains a separate upkeep trigger.

articles.era: 1996 World Championship Standard using current first-strike combat rules
articles.title: Three Plains, a first-strike block, and a fallen Juggernaut
articles.intro: Order of Leitbur is a two-white 2/1 with protection from black, activated first strike for {W}, and repeatable +1/+0 for {W}{W}. With spare white mana it can trade much higher than its base stats suggest.
articles.lesson: Order of Leitbur does not have first strike automatically. Paying {W} grants it first strike until end of turn; paying {W}{W} makes it 3/1 until end of turn. Protection from black is separate from the first-strike ability and does not protect against colorless artifact damage.
articles.origin: Bryon Wackwitz illustrated the original Order of Leitbur for Fallen Empires in 1994. Its mirror pairing with Order of the Ebon Hand highlighted the opposing white and black orders while placing combat math in activated abilities.
articles.technical: A previously controlled Order blocks an attacking Juggernaut (5/3). Before first-strike damage, tap three Plains for {W} to grant first strike and {W}{W} to raise power from two to three. The Order deals lethal three damage first; Juggernaut is destroyed before the normal combat damage step and never hits back.
articles.history: The Tom Chanpheng 1996 World Championship-winning white deck archive lists Order of Leitbur and Plains. The artifact attack is a representative constructed matchup, not an attributed feature match.
articles.story: My opponent attacked with [[Juggernaut]], a 5/3 that had to attack if able. I blocked with [[Order of Leitbur]], which had been under my control since the previous turn. I tapped three [[Plains]], using one white mana to give Order first strike and two to give it +1/+0. Now a 3/1 first striker, Order dealt three damage before regular combat damage and destroyed Juggernaut. Order lived because the dead attacker never dealt its five damage. I held [[Swords to Plowshares]] in reserve; the three-mana block had solved this combat without another spell.
articles.review: Order 2/1, spend W to grant first strike and WW for +1/+0. 3/1 first strike deals lethal 3 to artifact Juggernaut 5/3 before it hits back. Juggernaut may be blocked by non-Wall. Three Plains pay 3W, Swords in actual 1996 white deck.

articles.era: 1996 U.S. Nationals Mono-Black Necropotence representative play
articles.title: Three black mana changed a bad block
articles.intro: Order of the Ebon Hand mirrors the white Order's pump and first-strike structure in black, substituting protection from white for protection from black. A two-mana 2/1 can win combat if black mana remains available.
articles.lesson: The black Order gains first strike only after paying {B}, and each {B}{B} activation gives +1/+0. Its protection from white does not stop green or red creature damage, and its own black color cannot block creatures that have protection from black.
articles.origin: Melissa A. Benson illustrated Order of the Ebon Hand for Fallen Empires. The two rival orders were mechanically parallel despite different protections, carrying a competitive combat-mana puzzle into black aggro.
articles.technical: A 2/1 Order of the Ebon Hand can block a Kird Ape that is 2/3 because of Taiga's Forest type. Paying {B} and then {B}{B} grants first strike and +1/+0, making the Order 3/1. It kills the Ape during first-strike damage; the Ape deals no normal combat damage.
articles.history: Dennis Bentley's 1996 U.S. Nationals Necropotence deck archive includes Order of the Ebon Hand, Swamps, Hymn to Tourach and Necropotence. A Kird Ape opposing it in this scene is an era-correct hypothetical, not evidence of a particular real match.
articles.story: My opponent sent [[Kird Ape]] into combat with a [[Taiga]] in play, making the Ape a 2/3. I blocked with [[Order of the Ebon Hand]], my 2/1 black creature. Three untapped [[Swamp]]s gave me the choice to fight rather than lose the Order. I paid one black to give it first strike and two more to pump it to 3/1. Order struck for three first-strike damage and killed the Ape before the Ape could hit back. My [[Necropotence]] remained in play. Protection from white wasn't what won this fight; timing and black mana were.
articles.review: Kird Ape + Taiga Forest type -> 2/3. Order 2/1 spends B first strike and BB to pump 3/1, first strike lethal 3 against Ape; no normal retaliation. 3 Swamps and Necropotence in actual source deck.

articles.era: 2006 World Championship Standard representative Boros aggro game
articles.matchup: Boros aggro against green mana acceleration
articles.title: The counter left before the creature died
articles.intro: Icatian Javelineers is a one-white 1/1 that arrives with a single javelin counter, storing one targeted point of damage. Spending that counter and tapping the creature is an activated ability, not a free enters-the-battlefield trigger.
articles.lesson: Icatian Javelineers enters with one javelin counter. Activating its {T}, remove-a-counter ability is limited by summoning sickness on the turn it enters. Once activated, destroying Javelineers in response doesn't counter its already-stacked damage ability.
articles.origin: Melissa A. Benson illustrated Icatian Javelineers for Fallen Empires, bringing a single-use targeted damage effect to white weenie creature play.
articles.technical: If Javelineers has been under your control since the start of turn, tap it and remove its only javelin counter as costs to target an opposing Llanowar Elves. Even if an opponent kills Javelineers after activation, the ability normally still deals one on resolution, killing the 1/1 Elf.
articles.history: The 2006 Nicholas Lovett World Championship Boros deck archive lists Icatian Javelineers, Plains and Lightning Helix. The opposing green Elf and response are original illustrative board states.
articles.story: My [[Icatian Javelineers]] had entered last turn with one javelin counter. During my opponent's main phase I tapped it and removed that counter, targeting their [[Llanowar Elves]]. My opponent answered with [[Shock]], destroying the Javelineers while its ability remained on the stack. The ability still resolved and dealt one damage to the Elves, so the 1/1 died too. I still had [[Lightning Helix]] in hand, but I did not need to spend it on the mana creature. If I had just cast Javelineers this turn, its tap activation would not have been available yet.
articles.review: Javelineers under controller since preceding turn; tap and remove one counter as costs. Opponent Shock destroys Javelineers after activation; its damage ability persists and kills 1/1 Llanowar Elves. Hypothetical opponent, 2006 period card pool.

articles.matchup: Titania's Lock against white creature aggro
articles.title: The artifact was already gone when it dealt damage
articles.intro: Aeolipile converts a two-mana artifact into two targeted damage by paying one additional generic mana, tapping and sacrificing the artifact. The sacrifice occurs as an activation cost, not after the damage resolves.
articles.lesson: Pay {1}, tap, and sacrifice Aeolipile to activate it; the ability deals two damage to any target on resolution. Aeolipile can activate the turn it was cast because it is a noncreature artifact, barring other restrictions. Removing the artifact in response cannot undo an already paid sacrifice cost.
articles.origin: Heather Hudson illustrated Aeolipile for Fallen Empires. It supplied decks without red spells a reusable-in-color but single-use removal choice at the price of a full artifact card.
articles.technical: One Plains supplies the generic {1} for Aeolipile. Tap and sacrifice the artifact as additional activation costs, target an opposing White Knight (2/2), and on resolution deal two damage to destroy it. Destroying Aeolipile after activation is impossible; it already left the battlefield as a cost.
articles.history: George Baxter's 1996 Titania's Lock U.S. Nationals archival list includes Aeolipile in the main deck, alongside Winter Orb and Icy Manipulator. The opposing White Knight is a representative matchup, not a recorded match.
articles.story: My opponent attacked with [[White Knight]], a 2/2 first striker. I let it through combat, then before ending the turn tapped a [[Plains]] to pay one for [[Aeolipile]]. I tapped and sacrificed the artifact as the rest of the ability's cost, targeting the Knight after combat. When it resolved, Aeolipile dealt two damage and the Knight died. My [[Winter Orb]] was still on the table. The sacrifice happened before my opponent could respond to the activation; no spell that destroyed Aeolipile afterward could bring back a card I'd already paid as a cost.
articles.review: Aeolipile {1} tap sacrifice activation target opponent White Knight 2/2, two damage after combat lethal, cost paid Plains. Noncreature artifact tap not blocked by summoning sickness; opponent can respond to ability, artifact already gone.

articles.era: 1994 Fallen Empires kitchen-table red aggro teaching model
articles.title: The Goblin was gone before the answer arrived
articles.intro: Goblin Grenade turns a one-red-mana spell into five damage, but its sacrifice of a Goblin is an additional casting cost. The Goblin is gone before an opponent can respond to the spell.
articles.lesson: Goblin Grenade costs {R} plus sacrificing one Goblin. The sacrifice is made while casting, before the opponent gets priority to counter or remove the target. If the spell is countered, the sacrificed Goblin does not come back. The spell deals exactly five damage to one target if it resolves.
articles.origin: Ron Spencer illustrated the original 56a Goblin Grenade in Fallen Empires. It offers five damage for one red mana only by converting a Goblin permanent into a one-time additional cost; later red decks reused the same exchange.
articles.technical: With a Goblin already on the battlefield and an untapped Mountain, pay {R} and sacrifice that Goblin while casting Goblin Grenade. A later Counterspell can counter the spell but cannot stop the already-paid sacrifice; if the spell resolves against a player at five life, the damage is lethal.
articles.history: The inherited article had no verified deck registration. This migration creates a labeled 60-card 1994 Goblin teaching model using contemporaneous creatures, burn and Mountains. It is not a tournament deck or evidence of an event placement.
articles.story: I had [[Mons's Goblin Raiders]] on the battlefield and my opponent was at five life. During my main phase I tapped a [[Mountain]] for red mana, announced [[Goblin Grenade]] targeting them, and sacrificed the Raiders as an additional casting cost. My opponent held up blue mana for [[Counterspell]], but they could not destroy the sacrificed Goblin before I paid that cost. They let the spell resolve. Grenade dealt five damage and ended the game. I still had [[Lightning Bolt]] in hand, but the five-damage spell had done enough. The Goblin had gone to the graveyard before anyone could answer Grenade.
articles.review: Mons's Goblin Raiders is a Goblin. Mountain pays R; sacrifice Raiders is additional spell cost, occurs before priority response. Opponent has Counterspell but declines. Resolved spell deals 5 to 5-life player, lethal. All cards printed by 1994, fictitious deck.

articles.era: 1998 Pro Tour Rome Extended combo illustrated under current Oracle wording
articles.matchup: High Tide combo against Academy blue combo
articles.title: The first Island paid once; the others paid twice
articles.intro: High Tide is a one-blue-mana instant that makes Islands yield one additional blue mana whenever tapped for mana for the rest of the turn. It affects both players and any land with the Island subtype, not just basic Islands.
articles.lesson: An Island tapped to cast High Tide before the spell resolves gets no retroactive bonus. After it resolves, every subsequent Island tapped for mana provides the usual mana plus an additional {U} for the controller, including the opponent's Islands. Multiple High Tides can stack.
articles.origin: Drew Tucker illustrated the original 18a High Tide in Fallen Empires; other original art variants had Anson Maddocks and Amy Weber. Years later, 1998 Pro Tour Rome combo players exploited High Tide alongside Time Spiral, Turnabout and Stroke of Genius.
articles.technical: With four basic Islands, tap the first for {U} to cast High Tide. Once it resolves, tap Island #2 and #3 for {U}{U} apiece, accumulating {U}{U}{U}{U}. Cast Turnabout for {2}{U}{U} targeting yourself and choosing lands; untap all four Islands. Tapping all four afterwards yields eight blue mana (two apiece).
articles.history: Federico Dato's 1998 Pro Tour Rome High Tide archive includes Island, High Tide, Turnabout, Time Spiral, Merchant Scroll and Stroke of Genius. Wizards later described High Tide as a successful anti-Academy combo deck at that Pro Tour; this specific four-Island line remains an editorial reconstruction.
articles.story: I began my main phase with four [[Island]]s untapped and [[High Tide]] in hand. The first Island paid the single blue to cast Tide; it received no bonus because the spell had not resolved. After it resolved, I tapped two more Islands, each producing two blue, and spent all four to cast [[Turnabout]] targeting myself and choosing lands. All my Islands untapped. I then tapped all four for eight blue mana, enough to start working toward [[Stroke of Genius]]. My opponent could receive the same Island bonus on their own taps that turn. Tide was symmetrical, not a private enchantment.
articles.review: Four Islands. First taps for U to cast High Tide pre-resolution and no bonus. Second+third after resolution each produce UU -> total four blue for Turnabout {2}{U}{U}. Turnabout targets self and untaps lands including first three, fourth previously untapped. Four Islands afterwards produce 8 blue. Both players' Islands affected.
